content:
After God heard the prayer of Moses and pardoned the people, He continued speaking, and He made a very solemn declaration. He said, "As surely as I live, and as surely as the whole earth shall be filled with the glory of Yahweh, none of the men who have seen My glory and the signs which I performed in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tested Me these ten times and have not obeyed My voice, shall see the land which I swore to give to their fathers. None of those who have treated Me with contempt shall see it" (Numbers 14:21-23). These are among the most sobering words that Yahweh spoke in the whole wilderness journey. Although He had forgiven the nation in answer to the intercession of Moses, He declared that the unbelieving generation would not enter the Promised Land. Forgiveness did not remove the earthly consequences of their long and repeated rebellion. Their sin was pardoned, but the door to Canaan was closed to that generation.

Now notice carefully how Yahweh describes their sin. He does not merely say that they doubted Him, or that they complained against Him. He says that they had treated Him with contempt. This is a very strong word. Contempt means to despise, to scorn, to reject, or to treat someone as unworthy of respect or trust. It is far stronger than simply disliking someone. Contempt is the attitude that says, "I do not value you. I do not trust you. Your words do not matter to me." This is what God said about His own people. It is a heavy thing to consider, because Israel never once openly declared that they hated Yahweh.

They continued to travel with His people. They gathered around His tabernacle. They witnessed His miracles with their own eyes. And yet, in spite of all this, their actions revealed the true condition of their hearts.Their outward religion continued, but inwardly they were treating God as though His promises could not be trusted.

First, they treated Yahweh with contempt by refusing to trust His promises. God had promised again and again to give them the land of Canaan. This was not a small or unclear promise. It was repeated, certain, and backed by an oath. Yet after hearing the report of the ten spies, they believed the fearful words of men more than the faithful promise of God. Their unbelief was not caused by a lack of evidence. It was a refusal to trust the God who had never once failed them. When a person believes the fearful voices of men over the sure word of God, that is not merely weakness. In God's own eyes, it is contempt, because it treats His promise as worthless.

Second, they treated Yahweh with contempt by forgetting His mighty works. They had seen God deliver them out of Egypt. They had walked through the divided Red Sea on dry ground. They had eaten manna that fell from heaven every single morning. They had drunk water that came out of the rock.

They had been guided by the pillar of cloud during the day and the pillar of fire during the night. Yet when they stood at the border of Canaan, they behaved as though none of these miracles had ever happened. They ignored every proof of God's faithfulness. It is a serious thing to forget what God has done. When we forget His past kindness, we begin to doubt His present care, and we insult the very One who has carried us all along.

Third, their contempt became even clearer when they accused Yahweh of evil intentions. They asked, "Why is Yahweh bringing us into this land only to let us fall by the sword?" Instead of believing that God desired to bless them, they concluded that He intended to destroy them. They looked at the loving hand that had fed them and led them, and they said that this same hand was leading them to their deaths. They questioned His goodness. They doubted His love. This is one of the deepest forms of contempt, when a person takes the good intentions of God and calls them evil.

Fourth, they treated Yahweh with contempt by desiring to return to Egypt. They said among themselves that it would be better to go back to the land of their slavery. By rejecting Moses, whom God had appointed to lead them, they were in reality rejecting God's own leadership. They preferred the bondage of Egypt over trusting the God who had redeemed them with such a mighty hand. They even proposed choosing another leader to take them back into chains. To despise the freedom God has given, and to long for the very bondage from which He rescued us, is a great insult to His saving love.

Fifth, their rebellion reached its climax when they wanted to stone Joshua and Caleb. These two faithful men had spoken only what God had spoken.

They had not invented their message. They had simply repeated the promise of Yahweh. Yet the congregation wanted to silence them, because their words exposed the unbelief of the people. Rejecting God's faithful witnesses became another way of treating God Himself with contempt. When we try to silence the truth because it exposes our own unbelief, we are not merely opposing a messenger. We are opposing the God who sent the message.

Let us picture this in a simple way. Imagine a loving father who has faithfully cared for his child for many years. He has always kept his promises. He has never once failed to provide for his family. One day he says to his child, "Trust me. I will take care of you." But the child answers, "I do not believe you. I think you are trying to harm me." That father would be deeply wounded, not because the child asked a question, but because the child rejected years of proven love and faithfulness. This is exactly what Israel did to Yahweh. After everything He had done for them, they no longer trusted His heart. And this is why God called it contempt. It was not a small stumble. It was the settled rejection of a love that had been proven over and over again. Yet even here we must be careful, for there is a great difference between contempt and a genuine struggle of faith, and understanding that difference will be very important for us. But first, having seen how Israel treated God, we must turn the light upon our own hearts, for the same passage that describes Israel also searches us. That is where we will continue tomorrow.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,
We are sobered to see that Israel treated You with contempt while still traveling with Your people.

They saw Your wonders, yet believed the fears of men above Your faithful promise.

Guard our hearts from ever calling Your good intentions evil, or Your promises uncertain.

Help us to remember Your mighty works and never behave as though You have not helped us before.

You are a faithful Father who has proven Your love again and again; teach us to trust Your heart.

"I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your miracles of long ago." Psalm 77:11

In Christ name we pray. Amen.
